    In plain words

    The article describes research into Microsoft’s Windows Server Update Services, a system companies use to manage and send Windows updates to their computers. The author found that if this update system uses a separate Microsoft SQL database server, an attacker may be able to make the update server log in to that database and then use built-in database commands to create and send a harmful fake update. Organizations that run WSUS in this separated database setup are the ones affected. This matters because a tool meant to safely deliver trusted updates across a company could be turned into a way to place unwanted software on selected computers.

    Summary
    SpecterOps research shows that when WSUS uses a separate MSSQL database, an attacker can coerce and relay the WSUS server’s computer account to gain a SQL session and abuse WSUS stored procedures to create, target, and approve malicious updates. This could turn enterprise update infrastructure into a mechanism for lateral movement and payload deployment.

    The article presents Part 1 of SpecterOps research into Windows Server Update Services, a Windows server role used to manage Microsoft updates inside an organization. The author focused on whether control over WSUS or its database could be used to create and deploy custom malicious updates. The main finding is that if WSUS uses a separate standalone Microsoft SQL database, the upstream WSUS computer account can be coerced and relayed to that database to establish a SQL session.

    The author first tested relaying the upstream WSUS server to a downstream WSUS server over SMB, but found that the upstream server did not have administrative rights over the downstream server. Relaying the same upstream WSUS computer account to the WSUS SQL database succeeded, although the account had limited direct permissions in the SUSDB database. The account belonged to the webService database role, which lacked direct table permissions but had EXECUTE permissions over stored procedures.

    The article then walks through stored procedures that can be used to create, configure, target, and deploy a custom update. These include spImportUpdate, spSaveXMLFragment, spSetBatchURL, spCreateTargetGroup, spAddComputerToTargetGroup, and spDeployUpdate. By creating update metadata, setting file download locations, creating a target group, adding a specific computer, and deploying the update to that group, the author shows how WSUS database access can be used to target individual systems rather than the entire domain.

    • The attack path does not require broad direct database table permissions because the WSUS computer account can use stored procedures exposed through the webService database role to perform the needed update actions.
    • Relaying the upstream WSUS server to a downstream WSUS server was not useful in the author’s test because the upstream server lacked administrative rights there, but relaying the same account to the WSUS SQL database succeeded.
    • WSUS automatic approval logic can be relevant to malicious update creation because the article shows update metadata can reference categories such as Critical or Security, although the default automatic approval rule is not enforced by default.
    • The ability to create a new target group and add a single computer means the described technique can be used against selected systems instead of pushing a malicious update to every WSUS client.
    • The article shows that creating a deployable custom WSUS update depends on several specific XML fragments, and omitting spSaveXMLFragment caused malformed XML errors in the author’s testing.
    Key Points

In plain words

The article explains how a Microsoft update server used inside organizations, called WSUS, can be made to send a harmful fake update to employee computers. The author found that files ending in .txt or .esd can skip a normal trust check, allowing an untrusted program to be delivered and run. This matters because companies using WSUS could have their update system turned into a way to keep reinstalling unwanted software on their own computers, especially when automatic updates are enabled.

Summary
The article shows how WSUS can be abused to deploy malicious updates, including a signature-check bypass where payloads ending in .txt or .esd skip verification. Defenders should tightly restrict WSUS database access and monitor suspicious update-creation and deployment stored procedures.

The article continues a WSUS research series by showing the final deployment step for a custom malicious update using the spDeployUpdate stored procedure. After deployment, the author observed that WSUS attempted to download the Specter.exe payload but failed because the hosting server did not support the HTTP Range header required by Background Intelligent Transfer Service. A basic Python server with BITS support allowed the download process to proceed further.

The next blocker was WSUS file verification, which failed because the payload was not signed by a trusted digital signing certificate. The author examined WSUS logs, identified ContentSyncAgent as the component involved, and decompiled Microsoft.UpdateServices.ContentSyncAgent.dll with dnSpy. The VerifyFile function showed that files ending in .txt or .esd skip the CheckCertificateSignature function, allowing the digital signature requirement to be bypassed.

The author then created a payload named Ghost.txt, deployed it through WSUS, and saw that the file was successfully downloaded and verified. After manually triggering installation on a workstation, the author received a command-and-control callback, and later observed that the update redeployed after the process exited. The article notes that if the Configure Automatic Updates group policy is set to option 4, the update can install without user interaction, and recommends restricting WSUS database access and monitoring specific stored procedures such as spCreateTargetGroups, spSetBatchURL, and spDeployUpdate.

  • A WSUS payload does not need to be a Microsoft-signed binary if the update file name ends in .txt or .esd, because the WSUS verification logic skips the certificate-signature check for those extensions.
  • A simple web server may fail to host WSUS update payloads because WSUS requires BITS-compatible downloads with HTTP Range header support.
  • The malicious update can run without user interaction when the Configure Automatic Updates group policy is enabled with option 4, Auto download and schedule install.
  • The technique can act as persistence because the article observed the callback process exiting after a couple of hours and the update redeploying immediately afterward.
  • The article gives specific defensive database monitoring points, including spCreateTargetGroups, spSetBatchURL for .txt or .esd files, and spDeployUpdate from non-computer accounts.

  • 01The article continues from Part 1 by deploying a custom WSUS update through the spDeployUpdate stored procedure.
  • 02WSUS downloads update files through Background Intelligent Transfer Service, which requires the web server to support the HTTP Range header.
  • 03The author found that WSUS normally checks executable payloads for a trusted digital signature during file verification.
  • 04By decompiling Microsoft.UpdateServices.ContentSyncAgent.dll, the author found that files ending in .txt or .esd skip the CheckCertificateSignature function.

In plain words

OpenAI said it banned a coordinated group of ChatGPT accounts tied to a scam operation in Poipet, Cambodia, that used the tool to write and translate messages, create fake online identities, and make false documents for romance, investment, gambling, and police impersonation scams. The people affected include scam targets who may have been tricked into paying money, as well as workers recruited with false job promises and possibly forced into scam work. This matters because the operation shows how criminal groups can use AI tools to run many kinds of scams faster, across more people, and with more convincing fake stories.

Summary
OpenAI disrupted a Cambodia-based scam network in Poipet that used ChatGPT to create fake personas, translate victim messages, generate fraudulent documents, and support romance, investment, gambling, and law-enforcement impersonation scams. The case highlights how organized scam operations are using AI to scale and diversify fraud, potentially alongside human trafficking and forced labor.

OpenAI said it disrupted a Cambodia-based scam operation that used ChatGPT to support investment, romance, gambling, and law enforcement impersonation schemes. The company banned a coordinated network of ChatGPT accounts likely originating from Southeast Asia and operating from Poipet, a city the article links to scam compounds and human trafficking. OpenAI said it investigated the operation in partnership with Meta-owned WhatsApp.

The accounts used OpenAI’s models to create and support fake online personas, generate and translate messages sent to scam targets, and create promotional content for fraudulent schemes. Some accounts also used the tool for administrative work, including drafting internal announcements, translating staff messages, and documenting debts, salary deductions, fines, loan repayments, visa overstays, work permits, immigration status, and recruitment incentives. Promotional content included social media advertisements for “chatter” jobs in Poipet targeting users in Bangladesh and India with salary, travel, housing, meals, visa, and work permit offers.

OpenAI described the scammers’ process as a three-step “ping-zing-sting” approach, involving initial outreach on WhatsApp and Telegram, trust-building, and then demands for deposits, activation fees, or fake fines. The network used dating personas, fictitious investment experts, gambling platform representatives, and fraudulent law enforcement identities, and generated forged documents and fake screenshots. OpenAI said the operation may have interacted with hundreds of targets, with user conversations referencing individual victims losing thousands of dollars, although those claims were not independently verified.

  • The scam network used ChatGPT not only for victim-facing deception but also for internal business operations, including staff announcements, translations, debt tracking, salary deductions, fines, loan repayments, visa overstays, work permits, immigration status, and recruitment incentives.
  • The operation blended multiple scam types at the same time, showing that the same criminal infrastructure and personas were reused across romance, investment, gambling, and law enforcement impersonation schemes.
  • Recruitment ads for “chatter” jobs in Poipet targeted users in Bangladesh and India with unusually complete relocation offers, including flights, housing, meals, visas, and work permits.
  • OpenAI investigated the operation in partnership with Meta-owned WhatsApp, indicating that scam activity spanning AI tools and messaging platforms required cross-platform coordination to disrupt.
  • Some account activity was consistent with human trafficking and forced labor, linking the online scam operation to possible exploitation of recruited workers as well as financial fraud against victims.

COLDCARD security audit phishing attack installs remote access tool

In plain words

Scammers are sending fake COLDCARD emails that claim users must take part in a security audit after reports of a wallet flaw and a large Bitcoin theft. The emails lead people to a fake COLDCARD website and a downloaded “diagnostic” tool that secretly installs software giving the scammers control of the victim’s computer. People who use COLDCARD hardware wallets are the main targets, and the danger is that attackers could steal personal data or cryptocurrency, install more harmful software, or even use the access for ransomware.

Summary
A phishing campaign is impersonating COLDCARD’s security audit process to trick hardware wallet users into installing a fake diagnostic tool that deploys ConnectWise ScreenConnect for remote access. Attackers use a convincing website and live chat to pressure victims into approving the installation, potentially enabling theft of data or cryptocurrency.

A phishing campaign is exploiting fears around a recently disclosed COLDCARD wallet vulnerability and a suspected $88.6 million Bitcoin theft. Proofpoint says the campaign uses emails impersonating COLDCARD that claim a security audit is underway across its hardware cold storage wallet devices. The emails are sent from compliance@coldcardteamnews.com with the subject “Hardware audit now available” and direct recipients to a fake audit process.

The phishing site, coldcardcompliance.com, impersonates COLDCARD and prompts users to download a supposed “Security Verification & Incident Reporting Tool.” Proofpoint shared that the site’s “Start Hardware Audit” button downloads a batch file named Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool.bat from a GitHub account. BleepingComputer found that the script pretends to perform diagnostics while checking for administrator privileges, relaunching itself with a Windows prompt if needed, and decoding embedded files into the Windows temp folder.

The batch file installs a setup.msi file that is actually a ConnectWise ScreenConnect installer, while also launching a legitimate signed DocuSign executable as a decoy. Proofpoint says the ScreenConnect installer connects to activeretirementrelocation.com, the command-and-control server used by the threat actor. Once connected, the attackers could remotely access the computer, steal data or cryptocurrency, install additional malware, or use the access to deploy ransomware.

  • The lure explicitly reassures users that the process is air-gapped and will not request their recovery seed, showing the attackers tailored the message to overcome concerns that hardware wallet users would be expected to have.
  • The phishing site’s live chat appears to involve real operators who can answer questions and coach hesitant victims through administrator prompts, making the campaign more persuasive than a static phishing page.
  • The fake diagnostic tool uses a legitimate signed DocuSign executable as a decoy while installing ScreenConnect in the background, which could make the activity appear less suspicious to victims.
  • The batch file requests elevated Windows permissions by relaunching itself through PowerShell if needed, so an administrator prompt during the “audit” is a concrete warning sign described in the campaign.
  • The ScreenConnect server domain identified in the campaign is activeretirementrelocation.com, giving defenders and users a specific connection indicator to investigate.
Key Points
  • 01A phishing campaign is impersonating COLDCARD and claiming that a security audit is underway across its hardware cold storage wallet devices.
  • 02The campaign follows a suspected theft of approximately 1,367 Bitcoin, worth about $88.6 million, from 4,585 addresses using what is believed to be a random number generation flaw affecting multiple COLDCARD models and firmware versions.
  • 03The phishing emails direct users to coldcardcompliance.com, which impersonates COLDCARD and offers a fake “Security Verification & Incident Reporting Tool.”
  • 04Clicking the fake site’s “Start Hardware Audit” button downloads a batch file named Coldcard_Diagnostic_Tool.bat that pretends to run diagnostics while installing software in the background.
  • 05The installed MSI is a ConnectWise ScreenConnect installer that connects to activeretirementrelocation.com and can give the attackers remote access to the victim’s device.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a specific active phishing campaign using a fake COLDCARD audit tool to install ConnectWise ScreenConnect for remote access, with potential theft of cryptocurrency, data, or deployment of ransomware. It is especially relevant for security professionals because the article provides concrete indicators, delivery details, and user-interaction tactics used in the campaign.

In plain words

Researchers found online services, including one called Poison Claude, selling cheap access to AI systems from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI by secretly routing customers’ questions through other accounts. People who use these discount services are affected because the service operator can see everything they type and could leak or sell it, and the promised access might stop working or be worse than advertised. The broader concern is that these gray-market services help people get around access limits and may support wider misuse of AI, including in places where some U.S. AI tools are blocked or unavailable.

Summary
Okta researchers found gray-market services like Poison Claude selling cheap, unauthorized access to Anthropic and OpenAI models by proxying customer prompts through pooled accounts funded with free credits. These services can see every prompt customers send, creating major privacy and data-leak risks while access may be unreliable or fraudulent.

Cybersecurity researchers found more than half-a-dozen advertisements for illegal access to AI models on underground cybercrime forums and messaging platforms. One service, Poison Claude, claims to offer access to Anthropic models such as Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.6, and Sonnet 4.6. Okta researchers said the service offers cheap tokens by using free bonus credits, including AWS Bedrock account credits, and routing customer requests through pooled accounts.

Poison Claude accepts cryptocurrency payments and gives customers an Anthropic-compatible API key along with instructions to make Claude Code use Poison Claude’s API instead of Anthropic’s. Customer prompts are passed from Poison Claude’s API to Anthropic, and the responses are returned through the same path. Okta said this gateway setup gives the service provider full visibility into customer prompts, creating a privacy concern because data could be accidentally leaked or sold.

Okta said a configuration error exposed a Poison Claude API status endpoint that showed 881 total users and 872 active users before the issue was fixed. A similar gray-market service, Ecomagent.in, is estimated to have nearly 970 users and claims to offer discounted access to Anthropic models and OpenAI’s GPT Codex 5.5 through a custom API endpoint. The article says these services may attract users because of cost, access restrictions, privacy, or anonymity, but model providers may cut off fraudulent accounts or the services may provide cheaper and less capable models than advertised.

  • The privacy risk is central to these discount AI services because their proxy design requires every customer prompt to pass through the service provider before reaching the real model provider.
  • The exposed Poison Claude status endpoint suggested the service had hundreds of active users, with Okta reporting 881 total users and 872 active users before the issue was fixed.
  • Cloudflare placed a phishing warning in front of Poison Claude’s main site after disclosure, but Okta said the separate API domain remained behind Cloudflare Turnstile bot protection.
  • The article highlights that users may be drawn to these services for lower cost, access restrictions, privacy, or anonymity, but those same services may deliver weaker models or lose access if the underlying fraudulent accounts are cut off.
  • Okta connected the abuse of free AI trials with synthetic identity creation at scale using disposable domains, showing that the gray-market AI access issue overlaps with broader bot and fake-account activity.
Key Points
  • 01Okta researchers found more than half-a-dozen advertisements for illegal access to AI models on underground cybercrime forums and messaging platforms.
  • 02Poison Claude claims to offer discounted access to Anthropic models by routing customer requests through pooled accounts funded with free bonus credits, such as AWS Bedrock account credits.
  • 03After payment in cryptocurrency, Poison Claude gives customers an Anthropic-compatible API key and instructions to make Claude Code use the Poison Claude API instead of Anthropic’s API.
  • 04Okta said Poison Claude’s operators can see customer prompts because the service functions as a gateway that forwards prompts to the model provider.
  • 05A similar gray-market service, Ecomagent.in, claims to offer discounted access to Anthropic models and OpenAI’s GPT Codex 5.5 through a custom API endpoint.

Two Invoices, One Reference ID, and a $4.8 Trillion Typo
ironscales.com · 05 Aug 2026 11:00 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5
TAGSadobe-acrobat-procallback-phishingcisafbi-ic3google-workspaceimage-based-phishinginvoice-fraudironscales-themisspearphishing-attachmentspearphishing-voicevishing
78
In plain words

A home care and senior in-home care services company received a fake overdue invoice email that claimed a wildly impossible \(4.8 trillion balance, while the attached fake Adobe Acrobat invoice showed \)229.99 and pushed the reader to call a phone number shown only inside the image. The people affected were the company’s email recipient and anyone who might call the number, where a scammer could try to talk them into paying, sharing card details, giving access, or exposing banking information. It matters because this kind of scam avoids normal warning signs like suspicious links and relies on a convincing-looking picture and a live phone call to trick people.

Summary
A callback-phishing email impersonated an Adobe Acrobat invoice with no clickable links, hiding its only call to action as a phone number inside an image attachment. The mismatched trillion-dollar email amount, $229.99 invoice image, shared reference ID, and unfilled merge token exposed the scam as a broken but still dangerous phishing kit.

A mailbox at a home care and senior in-home care services company received an overdue-invoice notice claiming a balance of \(4,827,603,074,863. The attached JPEG invoice impersonated Adobe Acrobat and showed a much smaller grand total of \)229.99, while both the email body and image shared the same reference UUID. The article says this shared identifier shows the mismatched artifacts came from the same generation run rather than a simple wrong attachment.

The message contained zero links, and its only call to action was a toll-free phone number rendered three times as pixels inside the invoice image. The invoice also exposed a quality-control failure by leaving the unfilled merge-field placeholder #TFN1# in its refund-policy text. The article frames the case as callback phishing or vishing delivered through an attachment, where URL reputation and detonation had no input because there was nothing to click.

The sending domain had been registered roughly a year before the attack, used a mainstream workspace provider, passed DKIM, softfailed SPF, and had no DMARC record. IRONSCALES Themis scored the message at 87 percent confidence, labelled it credential theft, and the incident auto-resolved as phishing with one mailbox affected. The article recommends treating rendered attachment content as message content, comparing amounts across artifacts, and alerting on unrendered merge tokens.

  • The shared reference UUID across the mismatched email body and invoice image showed that the contradictory invoices were produced by the same tooling rather than caused by a simple wrong attachment.
  • Because the phone number appeared only inside the image and the message had zero URLs, defenses that rely on link extraction, URL reputation, detonation, or body-text matching had little direct material to evaluate.
  • The unfilled #TFN1# merge token, inconsistent amounts, and one reference ID spanning two invoice numbers are concrete fingerprints that defenders can use to identify related messages even if the sending domain changes.
  • The clean DKIM pass only proved that the sender controlled the attacker-registered domain on a mainstream workspace provider, while the SPF softfail and absent DMARC policy left authentication unable to establish trustworthiness.
  • The article recommends treating image text as message content by using optical character recognition, comparing amounts across email bodies and attachments, and alerting on unrendered merge tokens in delivered messages.
Key Points
  • 01A mailbox at a home care and senior in-home care services company received an overdue-invoice notice claiming a balance of $4,827,603,074,863.
  • 02The attached JPEG invoice impersonated Adobe Acrobat, showed a grand total of $229.99, and shared the same reference UUID as the email body despite using a different invoice number.
  • 03The message contained no links, and its only call to action was a toll-free phone number rendered three times as pixels inside the image attachment.
  • 04The invoice image included an unsubstituted merge-field placeholder, #TFN1#, in its refund-policy text, indicating a malfunctioning phishing kit.
  • 05IRONSCALES Themis scored the message at 87 percent confidence, and the incident auto-resolved as phishing with one mailbox affected.

JUSTIFICATION

This reports a specific real phishing event with broadly relevant defensive lessons around zero-URL callback scams, image-rendered phone numbers, and broken phishing-kit artifacts. It is not a major breach or urgent exploitation event, but it provides concrete indicators and actionable detection ideas for email security professionals.

Summary
Maksim Silnikau, the Belarusian creator and administrator of the Ransom Cartel ransomware operation, was sentenced to 16 years in U.S. prison for attacks on at least 18 organizations worldwide. Prosecutors said the group attempted to extort at least $5.2 million and caused more than $6.7 million in known victim losses.

Maksim Silnikau, a 40-year-old Belarusian national, was sentenced to 16 years in prison for his role as the creator and administrator of the Ransom Cartel ransomware operation. The U.S. Department of Justice said he was sentenced for conspiracy to commit offenses against the United States, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, and aggravated identity theft. Prosecutors said Ransom Cartel affiliates attacked at least 18 companies worldwide between 2021 and 2023 and attempted to extort at least $5.2 million from victims.

According to court documents, Silnikau began developing Ransom Cartel in May 2021 and recruited other cybercriminals through underground forums. He supplied members with stolen credentials and software used to encrypt victims’ computers, and he operated an affiliate website used to manage attacks, communicate, negotiate ransom demands, and distribute revenue shares. The operation stole corporate data and demanded payment for decryption keys or promises not to leak stolen information.

The United States identified more than \(6.7 million in losses among 18 known victims, with prosecutors saying the total was likely higher because some victims had not reported attacks. Reported incidents included a medical technology startup disrupted for two months and law firm infrastructure outages lasting from several days to multiple months, with two law firms paying ransoms of \)125,000 and $300,000. Silnikau was initially arrested in Spain in July 2023, fled while awaiting extradition, was later captured while trying to return to Belarus, and was ultimately extradited from Poland to the United States.

  • Ransom Cartel’s impact extended beyond ransom demands, with one medical technology startup disrupted for two months and law firm infrastructure outages lasting from several days to multiple months.
  • Researchers linked Ransom Cartel to REvil through shared code similarities, but missing REvil obfuscation features suggested it may have been built by someone without access to the full REvil source code.
  • Silnikau’s role covered multiple parts of the operation, including recruiting affiliates, coordinating with initial access brokers, communicating with victims, handling ransom payments, and using cryptocurrency mixers to obscure funds.
  • The known financial harm was likely incomplete because prosecutors said some victims had not reported their attacks, even though 18 identified victims already accounted for more than $6.7 million in losses.

In plain words

The article explains how AWS Nitro Enclaves can work with AWS Key Management Service to let protected cloud applications use encryption keys only when AWS verifies that the right enclave is asking. This matters because mistakes in setup can let a malicious host, insider, or misconfigured permission cause the enclave to use the wrong key, replay requests, expose secrets, or lose access to data. People and organizations building systems on AWS Nitro Enclaves and KMS are affected, especially if they rely on these services to protect sensitive information from the rest of the cloud environment.

Summary
AWS Nitro Enclaves can integrate with KMS for attestation-protected key access, but the enclave-KMS channel introduces serious risks unless requests use Recipient attestation, strict key policies, encryption context, hardcoded CMK ARNs, and enclave-initiated TLS. Even with correct cryptography, operational issues like policy mutability, key rotation, deletion, backups, quotas, and SDK safety must be carefully managed.

The article examines how AWS Nitro Enclaves integrate with AWS Key Management Service, focusing on the risks in the communication channel between enclaves and KMS. KMS can verify enclave attestation documents and restrict access to customer-managed keys based on PCR values. KMS can also encrypt supported operation responses to a public key included in an enclave attestation document.

The article explains that only some KMS operations support these enclave attestation mechanisms, including GenerateDataKey, GenerateDataKeyPair, Decrypt, DeriveSharedSecret, and GenerateRandom. The Encrypt operation does not support the attestation-based protections, so the article says enclave cryptographic operations are supposed to be implemented through data keys rather than directly through customer-managed keys. It also describes use cases such as authenticated external storage, signing enclave image files, and adding entropy with GenerateRandom.

The article catalogs passive and active attack classes, including data key swaps, incorrect CMK selection, replay of fresh attestation documents, side-channel observations, and request modification when traffic can be changed in transit. It recommends protections such as using the Recipient parameter, encryption context, hardcoded full CMK ARNs, validation of returned key IDs, enclave-initiated TLS with an attested CA set, and careful KMS key policies. It also highlights operational risks including key rotation and revocation, data key backup responsibility, CMK deletion, regional outages, billing abuse, quotas, eventual consistency, and avoiding aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c because the authors found vulnerabilities in it.

  • KMS attestation does not cover the Encrypt operation, so enclave designs that try to use CMKs directly for encryption will miss the attestation-based protections and should instead implement cryptographic operations through data keys.
  • The article warns that using key aliases instead of full CMK ARNs can let an attacker manipulate IAM credentials to make an enclave use a key in the wrong AWS account or Region.
  • Fresh Nitro Enclave attestation documents can be replayed within KMS’s five-minute validity window because KMS does not cryptographically bind the attestation to the rest of the request and does not use the attestation document’s user_data or nonce fields.
  • A KMS key policy that grants permissions to an account root principal can unintentionally allow any IAM role with matching IAM-policy access to operate on the key, even if the policy appears to restrict use to root and the enclave.
  • The article specifically recommends avoiding aws-nitro-enclaves-sdk-c because the authors found vulnerabilities in it that can be used to exploit enclaves from the parent host.
Key Points
  • 01AWS KMS can verify Nitro Enclave attestation documents and restrict customer-managed key access based on expected PCR values, while also encrypting supported operation responses to a public key included in the attestation document.
  • 02Only some KMS operations support enclave attestation mechanisms, including GenerateDataKey, GenerateDataKeyPair, Decrypt, DeriveSharedSecret, and GenerateRandom, while Encrypt does not support those attestation-based security mechanisms.
  • 03Passive attack risks include attacker-controlled encrypted data key swaps, incorrect or ambiguous CMK selection, replay of fresh attestation documents, side-channel leakage from communication timing and size, and attacker-controlled key specifications or algorithm identifiers.
  • 04The article states that active attacks require enclave-initiated TLS with an attested and limited CA set, ideally pinning Amazon’s KMS CA certificate, because attestation public keys are not bound to the rest of the KMS request.
  • 05Operational risks remain even when the cryptography is correct, including CMK rotation and revocation, data key rotation limitations because ReEncrypt does not support attestations, CMK deletion risks, regional outages, data key backups, billing abuse, quotas, size limits, and eventual consistency in KMS changes.

Prediction markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi can use public platform metrics to decide the outcome of bets. The article explains that metrics like Spotify streams, Twitch viewing hours, public votes, player counts, and crowdsourced leaderboard rankings are generated by user activity and can often be influenced by bots. This creates a financial incentive for traders to manipulate a metric without being connected to the platform, creator, streamer, song, game, or AI model receiving the artificial activity.

The article discusses a Spotify case involving Malcolm Todd’s song “Earrings,” which briefly reached the top of Spotify’s daily US chart while a Kalshi market asked whether he would have a number-one Spotify USA song before the end of June. Spotify later removed more than 500,000 artificial streams and corrected the chart position from first to fourth, but Kalshi had already resolved the market using the initial chart. The article uses this example to show how a market can settle before a platform finishes detecting and correcting artificial activity.

The article also examines AI leaderboards, Twitch viewing hours, Reddit votes, Roblox player counts, GitHub stars, YouTube views, Discord reactions, app-store rankings, online games, and public polls as potential targets. It argues that the riskiest combination is a large market, a close outcome, a user-generated metric, and a precise resolution time. Platforms may absorb fake traffic, distorted analytics, recommendation effects, infrastructure costs, moderation work, and investigations even though they did not agree to serve as a settlement source for a financial market.

  • The attacker’s goal may be temporary visibility rather than lasting manipulation, because a metric only needs to remain uncorrected until the prediction market’s resolution snapshot.

  • Repeated use of the same platform metrics in prediction-market rules can make account farms and automation infrastructure more valuable, because attackers can amortize setup costs across multiple future bets.
  • Post-vote reveal mechanisms on crowdsourced AI leaderboards can help attackers build labeled examples of model behavior, making targeted voting easier even when models are initially anonymous.
  • Prediction-market platforms can reduce manipulation incentives by limiting market size relative to estimated attack cost, delaying settlement during fraud review, and defining what happens if the source platform later corrects the metric.

In plain words

The article explains how a stolen work username and password can let criminals get into a company and, within about 72 hours, move from logging in to stealing information or locking systems for ransom. Employees and organizations are affected because stolen company logins are bought and sold on hidden online markets, often before the company knows there is a problem. The real-world risk is that delayed discovery can make the damage, investigation, costs, and reporting obligations much worse.

Summary
Stolen credentials can let attackers progress from initial login to persistence, lateral movement, data theft, and ransomware within 72 hours. Early detection of exposed credentials and abnormal identity activity is critical to stopping a breach before major business impact.

The article explains how a single stolen username and password can lead to a full cybersecurity incident within 72 hours. It describes how credentials exposed through phishing campaigns, malware infections, infostealers, or data breaches are traded on underground forums and dark web marketplaces. Once attackers obtain valid credentials, they may move quickly from unauthorized login to privilege abuse, lateral movement, data exfiltration, and ransomware deployment.

Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs reported monitoring more than 6,046 confirmed data breach incidents globally in 2025, with stolen credentials and compromised identities remaining common starting points for enterprise attacks. The article also states that more than 50 active infostealer variants are circulating and harvesting usernames, passwords, browser cookies, and session tokens. Because attackers use legitimate credentials, they can often bypass traditional perimeter defenses without immediately triggering alarms.

The article breaks the intrusion into stages: initial access in hours 0–6, persistence in hours 6–18, privilege escalation and internal reconnaissance in hours 18–36, lateral movement in hours 36–60, and data exfiltration and business impact in hours 60–72. It highlights detection opportunities such as unfamiliar logins, impossible travel events, unexpected MFA changes, excessive directory queries, abnormal service account usage, large outbound transfers, and encryption activity across multiple endpoints. It argues that early visibility into exposed credentials and rapid response can help organizations interrupt credential-based attacks before they become business-wide crises.

  • The article emphasizes that valid credentials can let attackers bypass traditional perimeter defenses because they are logging in rather than exploiting software vulnerabilities.
  • Persistence can survive a password reset if attackers add new authentication methods, change MFA settings, create additional accounts, or generate persistent API tokens.
  • Minor identity and administration changes, such as unexpected MFA updates, unauthorized mailbox rules, or changes to authentication configurations, may be the earliest signs that attackers are trying to stay inside the environment.
  • The article identifies the privilege escalation and internal reconnaissance window, from hour 18 to hour 36, as one of the strongest opportunities to stop attackers before they reach mission-critical assets.
  • Dark web monitoring is presented as a way to act before attackers even attempt to authenticate, because stolen corporate credentials may appear on underground marketplaces before the organization realizes there is a compromise.
Key Points
  • 01The article describes a 72-hour timeline in which attackers can use stolen credentials to progress from an unauthorized login to persistence, privilege escalation, lateral movement, data exfiltration, and possible ransomware deployment.
  • 02Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs reported monitoring more than 6,046 confirmed data breach incidents globally in 2025, with stolen credentials and compromised identities remaining common starting points for enterprise attacks.
  • 03During the first 6 hours, attackers may use credentials from dumps, phishing campaigns, malware infections, or reused passwords from breached third-party services to gain initial access.
  • 04Between hours 6 and 36, attackers may establish persistence by changing authentication settings or creating accounts, then expand access by enumerating Active Directory, identifying privileged users, scanning internal assets, and searching sensitive repositories.
  • 05Between hours 36 and 72, attackers may move across endpoints, servers, and cloud workloads, identify valuable information, exfiltrate sensitive data, and in many cases deploy ransomware afterward.

40
In plain words

HashiCorp, Veeam, and the Django Software Foundation fixed 11 security problems in Terraform MCP Server, Veeam Service Provider Console, and Django. The issues affect certain shared Terraform MCP setups, version 9 builds of Veeam’s service-provider backup console before 9.3, and some Django sites using geographic data features. In the worst cases, one user’s access could be wrongly reused by another, an attacker could get backup agent credentials, or a staff user could cause a server to write a file and possibly run code. The fixes are available now, and the article says there is no known active abuse of these flaws as of August 5, 2026.

Summary
HashiCorp, Veeam, and Django patched 11 vulnerabilities, including a CVSS 10.0 cross-tenant token reuse flaw in Terraform MCP Server, critical Veeam Service Provider Console bugs, and a high-severity GeoDjango issue that could lead to file writes or code execution. Operators should upgrade to Terraform MCP Server 1.1.0+, Veeam Service Provider Console 9.3.0.35057, and Django 6.0.8 or 5.2.17.

HashiCorp, Veeam, and the Django Software Foundation patched 11 vulnerabilities across Terraform MCP Server, Veeam Service Provider Console, and Django. The most serious issues include a Veeam flaw that can let an unauthenticated attacker impersonate a managed agent and obtain its credentials, a HashiCorp cross-tenant token reuse flaw scored CVSS 10.0, and a GeoDjango spatial lookup issue that can write a file to disk and may lead to code execution in some setups. Operators are advised to update Terraform MCP Server to version 1.1.0 or later, Veeam Service Provider Console to 9.3.0.35057, and Django to 6.0.8 or 5.2.17.

Exposure depends on configuration and product version. HashiCorp’s flaws affect Streamable HTTP deployments rather than stdio mode, Veeam’s flaws affect version 9 builds before 9.3, and Django’s documented admin attack path requires a staff user with view permission on a registered model containing a spatial field. The article notes that none of the advisories says the flaws are under active exploitation, none of the 11 CVEs appeared in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of August 5, 2026, and no public proof-of-concept had surfaced.

The HashiCorp issues involve credential isolation failures in Terraform MCP Server’s HTTP transport, including stateless mode reusing one user’s Terraform token for later users and stateful mode relying only on an MCP session ID. Veeam’s fixes include two critical flaws and two high-severity bugs in Service Provider Console, while Django’s release fixes one high-severity GeoDjango issue and three lower-severity issues involving stored cross-site scripting, denial of service, and memory consumption. The article also notes that Django’s GIS code had already drawn attacker attention earlier in the year after exploitation of a separate PostGIS raster lookup flaw.

  • The highest CVSS number is not necessarily the most urgent issue for every operator, because HashiCorp’s CVSS 10.0 flaw affects deliberately enabled stateless HTTP mode, while the lower-scored CVE-2026-16496 affects the default stateful mode for central deployments.
  • The Veeam flaw rated 9.5 requires no login but is not described as easy to exploit, because its CVSS vector rates attack complexity as high.
  • Terraform MCP Server deployments using only stdio mode are unaffected by the HashiCorp flaws, so exposure depends heavily on whether the server is run in shared Streamable HTTP mode.
  • The Django GeoDjango issue has a documented path through the admin interface, but that path requires a staff account with view permission on a registered model containing a spatial field.
  • There is a published affected-version discrepancy for Terraform MCP Server, with HashiCorp’s umbrella bulletin listing versions 0.2.1 through 1.0.0 while individual CVE records begin at 0.3.0, though both agree that 1.1.0 is the first fixed release.
Key Points
  • 01HashiCorp, Veeam, and the Django Software Foundation patched 11 vulnerabilities across Terraform MCP Server, Veeam Service Provider Console, and Django.
  • 02Veeam fixed four flaws in Veeam Service Provider Console build 9.3.0.35057, including CVE-2026-58073, an unauthenticated issue rated 9.5 that can let an attacker impersonate a managed agent and obtain that agent’s credentials.
  • 03HashiCorp fixed three Streamable HTTP transport flaws in Terraform MCP Server version 1.1.0, including CVE-2026-16498, a CVSS 10.0 cross-tenant credential-reuse bug in stateless HTTP mode.
  • 04Django released versions 6.0.8 and 5.2.17 to fix four CVEs, including CVE-2026-15307 in GeoDjango spatial lookups, which could write a file to disk or cause a network request and may lead to remote code execution in some setups.
  • 05None of the three advisories says the flaws are under active exploitation, and as of August 5, 2026, none of the eleven CVEs appears in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

payloads concept

payment method concept

persistence concept
Persistence is the ability for an attacker to keep access to a system over time.
personal data concept

personal details concept

personal information concept

personally identifiable information concept

phishing campaigns technique

phishing emails technique

phishing pages technique

phishing sites concept

phone numbers concept

plugin traffic concept

poland other
Poland is a country in Europe.

Policy enforcement means making sure rules, such as security or access rules, are actually applied.

private data concept
